purpose: Colchicine is mainly used to treat and prevent gout attacks, which cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling — most often in the big toe. It is also used to treat a condition called familial Mediterranean fever, which causes recurring episodes of fever and inflammation. Your doctor may occasionally prescribe it for other inflammatory conditions as well.
how_it_works: When you have a gout attack, uric acid crystals build up in your joints and trigger your immune cells to rush to the area and cause painful inflammation. Colchicine works by stopping those immune cells from moving into the joint and releasing the chemicals that cause swelling and pain. Think of it as putting up a roadblock so the inflammation cannot get out of control.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach-related and include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramps or pain. These are more likely to happen if you take a higher dose. If you get severe diarrhea, let your doctor know right away.
warnings: Colchicine can interact with many common medications — including certain antibiotics, cholesterol drugs like statins, and antifungals — so always tell your pharmacist and doctor everything you take. Taking too much colchicine can be very dangerous, even life-threatening, so never take more than prescribed. People with kidney or liver problems may need a lower dose. In rare cases, long-term use can affect your muscles or blood counts, so your doctor may monitor you with blood tests.
typical_dosing: For a gout flare, a common dosing schedule is 1.2 mg (two tablets) at the first sign of an attack, followed by 0.6 mg (one tablet) one hour later — do not take more than that in a 24-hour period unless your doctor tells you otherwise. For gout prevention, a typical dose is 0.6 mg once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as the right dose depends on your situation and other medications you take.
